title: Die Eule
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 174. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, gieng, Muth, gerathen, Ungethüm).
about: KHM 174 is a comic tale of mass hysteria: a great owl strays into a townsman's barn by night, and when the terrified servant mistakes it for a nameless monster, the whole town works itself into a panic over a creature no one dares look at closely. Volunteers arm themselves, a hired champion loses his nerve at the door, and the council finally solves the problem by paying off the barn's owner and burning the building down with the owl still inside — a small satire on crowds and cowardice, closer to a folk joke than to a magic tale.

sentences.t: Vor ein paar hundert Jahren, als die Leute noch lange nicht so klug und verschmitzt waren, als sie heutzutage sind, hat sich in einer kleinen Stadt eine seltsame Geschichte zugetragen.
sentences.l: A few hundred years ago, when people were by no means as clever and cunning as they are nowadays, a strange story took place in a little town.
sentences.i: A few hundred years ago, when people were nowhere near so clever and sly as they are today, a strange thing happened in a little town.
sentences.n: “noch lange nicht so … als” = ‘by no means as … as’ (the old comparative uses “als” where modern German uses “wie”). “hat sich … zugetragen” — sich zutragen, ‘to come to pass.’

sentences.t: Von Ungefähr war eine von den großen Eulen, die man Schuhu nennt, aus dem benachbarten Walde bei nächtlicher Weile in die Scheuer eines Bürgers gerathen und wagte sich, als der Tag anbrach, aus Furcht vor den andern Vögeln, die wenn sie sich blicken läßt, ein furchtbares Geschrei erheben, nicht wieder aus ihrem Schlupfwinkel heraus.
sentences.l: By chance one of the great owls that are called Schuhu had got, from the neighboring forest at nighttime, into a townsman’s barn, and, when the day broke, out of fear of the other birds — which, whenever it shows itself, raise a fearful clamor — did not venture out of its hiding-place again.
sentences.i: By chance one of the great owls that people call Schuhu had strayed from the neighboring wood in the night into a townsman’s barn, and when day broke it did not dare come out of its hiding-place again, for fear of the other birds, which raise a fearful outcry whenever it shows itself.
sentences.n: “Von Ungefähr” = ‘by chance.’ “Schuhu” is a folk name for the eagle-owl, from its cry. “gerathen” (1857 spelling of geraten) here = ‘to get, stray into.’ “wagte sich … nicht … heraus” — sich herauswagen, ‘to venture out.’

sentences.t: Als nun der Hausknecht Morgens in die Scheuer kam um Stroh zu holen, erschrack er bei dem Anblick der Eule, die da in einer Ecke saß, so gewaltig, daß er fortlief und seinem Herrn ankündigte ein Ungeheuer, wie er Zeit seines Lebens keins erblickt hätte, säße in der Scheuer, drehte die Augen im Kopf herum und könnte einen ohne Umstände verschlingen.
sentences.l: When now the house-servant came into the barn in the morning to fetch straw, he took such a mighty fright at the sight of the owl, which sat there in a corner, that he ran off and announced to his master that a monster, such as he had never seen in all his life, was sitting in the barn, rolled its eyes around in its head, and could swallow a man without ceremony.
sentences.i: Now when the house-servant came into the barn in the morning to fetch straw, he was so mightily frightened at the sight of the owl sitting there in a corner that he ran off and told his master a monster, such as he had never seen in all his life, was sitting in the barn, rolling its eyes about in its head and able to swallow a man on the spot.
sentences.n: “erschrack … so gewaltig, daß” — erschrecken, ‘to take fright.’ “ankündigte … säße” — the reported clause takes the subjunctive “säße” (‘was sitting’). “ohne Umstände” = ‘without ceremony, on the spot.’

sentences.t: „Ich kenne dich schon,“ sagte der Herr, „einer Amsel im Felde nachzujagen, dazu hast du Muth genug, aber wenn du ein todtes Huhn liegen siehst, so holst du dir erst einen Stock, ehe du ihm nahe kommst.
sentences.l: “I know you well,” said the master, “to chase a blackbird in the field, for that you have courage enough, but when you see a dead hen lying, you first fetch yourself a stick before you come near it.
sentences.i: “I know you all too well,” said the master, “to chase a blackbird in the field — for that you have pluck enough — but when you see a dead hen lying there, you first go and fetch a stick before you’ll go near it.
sentences.n: “Ich kenne dich schon” — here mocking, ‘I know your sort.’ “dazu hast du Muth genug” — the fronted “dazu” (‘for that’) resumes the preceding infinitive. “todtes” is the 1857 spelling of totes (dead). “du” is ‘you.’

sentences.t: Ich muß nur selbst einmal nachsehen was das für ein Ungeheuer ist“ setzte der Herr hinzu, gieng ganz tapfer zur Scheuer hinein und blickte umher.
sentences.l: I must just take a look myself for once at what kind of monster that is,” the master added, went quite bravely into the barn, and looked around.
sentences.i: I must just go and see for myself what sort of monster this is,” the master added, and went boldly into the barn and looked about him.
sentences.n: “nur … einmal” soften to ‘just once.’ “was das für ein … ist” — “was für ein” = ‘what kind of.’ “setzte … hinzu” — hinzusetzen, ‘to add.’ “gieng” = ging.

sentences.t: Als er aber das seltsame und greuliche Thier mit eigenen Augen sah, so gerieth er in nicht geringere Angst als der Knecht.
sentences.l: But when he saw the strange and gruesome creature with his own eyes, then he fell into no less fear than the servant.
sentences.i: But when he saw the strange, gruesome creature with his own eyes, he was seized with no less terror than the servant had been.
sentences.n: “greuliche” = ‘gruesome, horrible’ (1857 spelling of gräuliche). “gerieth in … Angst” — in Angst geraten, ‘to be seized with fear.’ “nicht geringere … als” = ‘no less … than.’

sentences.t: Mit ein paar Sätzen sprang er hinaus, lief zu seinen Nachbarn und bat sie flehentlich ihm gegen ein unbekanntes und gefährliches Thier Beistand zu leisten;
sentences.l: With a couple of bounds he sprang out, ran to his neighbors, and begged them beseechingly to lend him aid against an unknown and dangerous creature;
sentences.i: With a few bounds he leaped out, ran to his neighbors, and beseechingly begged them to help him against an unknown and dangerous beast;
sentences.n: “Mit ein paar Sätzen” — “Sätze” here are ‘bounds, leaps’ (from setzen, to spring), not ‘sentences.’ “flehentlich” = ‘beseechingly.’ “Beistand leisten” = ‘to render aid.’

sentences.t: ohnehin könnte die ganze Stadt in Gefahr kommen, wenn es aus der Scheuer, wo es säße, herausbräche.
sentences.l: in any case the whole town could come into danger if it broke out of the barn where it was sitting.
sentences.i: the whole town, he said, might be in danger if it broke out of the barn where it sat.
sentences.n: “ohnehin” = ‘in any case, anyway.’ “säße … herausbräche” — subjunctives (‘was sitting … broke out’) in the reported warning; herausbrechen, ‘to break out.’

sentences.t: Es entstand großer Lärm und Geschrei in allen Straßen: die Bürger kamen mit Spießen Heugabeln Sensen und Äxten bewaffnet herbei als wollten sie gegen den Feind ausziehen:
sentences.l: There arose great noise and clamor in all the streets: the townsfolk came up armed with spears, pitchforks, scythes, and axes, as if they meant to march out against the enemy:
sentences.i: A great noise and outcry arose in all the streets: the townsfolk came up armed with spears, pitchforks, scythes, and axes, as though they were marching out against an enemy:
sentences.n: “Es entstand” — impersonal ‘there arose.’ The source lists the weapons without commas (Spießen Heugabeln Sensen und Äxten). “als wollten sie … ausziehen” — ‘as if they wanted to march out’ (subjunctive, verb-first).

sentences.t: zuletzt erschienen auch die Herrn des Raths mit dem Bürgermeister an der Spitze.
sentences.l: at last the gentlemen of the council too appeared, with the burgomaster at their head.
sentences.i: at last the councillors themselves appeared, the burgomaster at their head.
sentences.n: “die Herrn des Raths” — “Raths” is the 1857 spelling of Rats (council). “Bürgermeister” = burgomaster, mayor. “an der Spitze” = ‘at the head.’

sentences.t: Als sie sich auf dem Markt geordnet hatten, zogen sie zu der Scheuer und umringten sie von allen Seiten.
sentences.l: When they had drawn themselves up in order on the market-square, they marched to the barn and surrounded it on all sides.
sentences.i: When they had formed up on the market-square, they marched on the barn and surrounded it on every side.
sentences.n: “sich geordnet hatten” — sich ordnen, ‘to draw up in order.’ “zogen” — ziehen, here ‘to march.’ “umringten” — umringen, ‘to surround.’

sentences.t: Hierauf trat einer der beherztesten hervor und gieng mit gefälltem Spieß hinein, kam aber gleich darauf mit einem Schrei und todtenbleich wieder heraus gelaufen, und konnte kein Wort hervor bringen.
sentences.l: Thereupon one of the boldest stepped forward and went in with leveled spear, but came running back out again right after with a cry and death-pale, and could not bring out a single word.
sentences.i: Thereupon one of the boldest stepped forward and went in with his spear leveled, but came running straight back out with a cry, white as death, and could not utter a word.
sentences.n: “Hierauf” = ‘thereupon.’ “mit gefälltem Spieß” — “gefällt” (from fällen) = ‘lowered, leveled’ (of a weapon). “todtenbleich” = ‘death-pale’ (1857 spelling). “hervor bringen” — hervorbringen, ‘to utter.’

sentences.t: Noch zwei andere wagten sich hinein, es ergieng ihnen aber nicht besser.
sentences.l: Two others still ventured in, but it went no better for them.
sentences.i: Two more ventured in, but they fared no better.
sentences.n: “wagten sich hinein” — sich hineinwagen, ‘to venture in.’ “es ergieng ihnen … nicht besser” — jemandem ergehen, ‘to fare’; ergieng is the 1857 spelling of erging.

sentences.t: Endlich trat einer hervor, ein großer starker Mann, der wegen seiner Kriegsthaten berühmt war, und sprach „mit bloßen Ansehen werdet ihr das Ungethüm nicht vertreiben, hier muß Ernst gebraucht werden, aber ich sehe daß ihr alle zu Weibern geworden seid und keiner den Fuchs beißen will.“
sentences.l: At last one stepped forward, a big strong man who was famous for his war-deeds, and said, “with mere looking you will not drive off the monster; here earnestness must be used, but I see that you have all turned into women and none wants to bite the fox.”
sentences.i: At last one came forward, a big strong man famous for his feats in war, and said, “you’ll not drive the beast off by just looking at it; here we must be in earnest — but I see you’ve all turned into women, and not one of you will bite the fox.”
sentences.n: “Kriegsthaten” = ‘war-deeds’ (Thaten is the 1857 spelling of Taten). “mit bloßen Ansehen” = ‘by mere looking.’ “den Fuchs beißen” — a taunting idiom, roughly ‘take the beast on, face the danger.’ “ihr” is plural ‘you.’

sentences.t: Er ließ sich Harnisch Schwert und Spieß bringen, und rüstete sich.
sentences.l: He had armor, sword, and spear brought to him and equipped himself.
sentences.i: He had armor, sword, and spear brought, and armed himself.
sentences.n: “ließ sich … bringen” — lassen + infinitive, ‘had (something) brought.’ “Harnisch” = harness, armor. “rüstete sich” — sich rüsten, ‘to arm oneself.’

sentences.t: Alle rühmten seinen Muth, obgleich viele um sein Leben besorgt waren.
sentences.l: All praised his courage, although many were anxious for his life.
sentences.i: Everyone praised his courage, though many feared for his life.
sentences.n: “rühmten” — rühmen, ‘to praise.’ “obgleich” = although. “um sein Leben besorgt” = ‘anxious for his life.’

sentences.t: Die beiden Scheuerthore wurden aufgethan, und man erblickte die Eule, die sich indessen in die Mitte auf einen großen Querbalken gesetzt hatte.
sentences.l: The two barn-doors were thrown open, and one caught sight of the owl, which had meanwhile seated itself in the middle on a great crossbeam.
sentences.i: The two barn-doors were thrown open, and there was the owl, which had meanwhile settled in the middle on a great crossbeam.
sentences.n: “Scheuerthore” = barn-doors (Thore is the 1857 spelling of Tore). “wurden aufgethan” — passive of aufthun (auftun), ‘to open.’ “indessen” = ‘meanwhile.’ “Querbalken” = crossbeam.

sentences.t: Er ließ eine Leiter herbeibringen, und als er sie anlegte und sich bereitete hinaufzusteigen, so riefen ihm alle zu er solle sich männlich halten, und empfahlen ihn dem heiligen Georg, der den Drachen getödtet hatte.
sentences.l: He had a ladder brought over, and as he set it up and prepared to climb up, all called out to him that he should hold himself manfully, and commended him to Saint George, who had slain the dragon.
sentences.i: He had a ladder fetched, and as he set it up and made ready to climb, they all called to him to bear himself like a man, and commended him to Saint George, who had slain the dragon.
sentences.n: “herbeibringen” = ‘to bring over.’ “riefen ihm … zu … er solle” — zurufen + reported command with “solle.” “sich männlich halten” = ‘to bear oneself manfully.’ Saint George is the dragon-slayer of legend.

sentences.t: Als er bald oben war, und die Eule sah daß er an sie wollte, auch von der Menge und dem Geschrei des Volks verwirrt war und nicht wußte wohinaus, so verdrehte sie die Augen, sträubte die Federn, sperrte die Flügel auf, gnappte mit dem Schnabel und ließ ihr schuhu, schuhu mit rauher Stimme hören.
sentences.l: When he was nearly up, and the owl saw that he meant to get at it, and was moreover confused by the crowd and the clamor of the people and did not know which way out, then it rolled its eyes, ruffled up its feathers, spread its wings open, snapped with its beak, and let its schuhu, schuhu be heard in a rough voice.
sentences.i: When he was nearly up, and the owl saw that he meant to get at it — bewildered too by the crowd and the people’s uproar, and not knowing which way to turn — it rolled its eyes, bristled its feathers, spread its wings, snapped its beak, and gave out its schuhu, schuhu in a harsh voice.
sentences.n: “daß er an sie wollte” — an jemanden wollen, ‘to mean to get at someone.’ “Volks” = of the people (Volk). “wohinaus” = ‘which way out.’ “gnappte” — gnappen, a dialect verb, ‘to snap (the beak).’ “schuhu” imitates the owl’s call.

sentences.t: „Stoß zu, stoß zu!“ rief die Menge draußen dem tapfern Helden zu.
sentences.l: “Thrust at it, thrust at it!” the crowd outside called to the brave hero.
sentences.i: “Strike, strike!” the crowd outside called to the brave hero.
sentences.n: “Stoß zu” — zustoßen, ‘to thrust, strike at.’ “dem tapfern Helden … zu … rief” — zurufen (+ dat.), ‘to call out to.’

sentences.t: „Wer hier stände, wo ich stehe,“ antwortete er, „der würde nicht stoß zu rufen.“
sentences.l: “Whoever stood here, where I stand,” he answered, “would not call ‘thrust at it.’”
sentences.i: “Anyone standing here, where I stand,” he answered, “would not be calling ‘strike.’”
sentences.n: “Wer hier stände” — subjunctive “stände” in the conditional, ‘whoever might stand.’ The inner citation “stoß zu” echoes the crowd’s shout.

sentences.t: Er setzte zwar den Fuß noch eine Staffel höher, dann aber fieng er an zu zittern und machte sich halb ohnmächtig auf den Rückweg.
sentences.l: He did indeed set his foot one rung higher, but then he began to tremble and made his way, half in a faint, back down.
sentences.i: He did set his foot one rung higher, but then he began to tremble and made his way back down, half fainting.
sentences.n: “zwar … aber” = ‘indeed … but.’ “Staffel” here = a rung or step of the ladder. “fieng an” — anfangen (fieng = fing). “machte sich … auf den Rückweg” — ‘set out on the way back.’ “halb ohnmächtig” = ‘half-fainting.’

sentences.t: Nun war keiner mehr übrig, der sich in die Gefahr hätte begeben wollen.
sentences.l: Now no one more was left who would have wanted to put himself into the danger.
sentences.i: Now there was no one left who would have been willing to face the danger.
sentences.n: “keiner mehr übrig” = ‘no one left.’ “sich in die Gefahr begeben” — sich begeben, ‘to put oneself into, face.’ “hätte … wollen” — past subjunctive, ‘would have wanted to.’

sentences.t: „Das Ungeheuer,“ sagten sie, „hat den stärksten Mann, der unter uns zu finden war, durch sein Gnappen und Anhauchen allein vergiftet und tödtlich verwundet, sollen wir andern auch unser Leben in die Schanze schlagen?“
sentences.l: “The monster,” said they, “has, by its snapping and breathing alone, poisoned and mortally wounded the strongest man that was to be found among us; are we others too to throw our lives into the venture?”
sentences.i: “The monster,” they said, “has, by its snapping and its breath alone, poisoned and mortally wounded the strongest man to be found among us — are the rest of us to stake our lives as well?”
sentences.n: “Gnappen und Anhauchen” — nominalized verbs, ‘snapping and breathing on.’ “tödtlich” = ‘mortally’ (1857 spelling). “sein Leben in die Schanze schlagen” is an idiom, ‘to risk, stake one’s life.’

sentences.t: Sie rathschlagten was zu thun wäre, wenn die ganze Stadt nicht sollte zu Grunde gehen.
sentences.l: They took counsel over what was to be done, if the whole town was not to go to ruin.
sentences.i: They deliberated over what should be done, if the whole town was not to be ruined.
sentences.n: “rathschlagten” — rathschlagen (1857 spelling of ratschlagen), ‘to take counsel, deliberate.’ “zu Grunde gehen” = ‘to go to ruin, perish.’

sentences.t: Lange Zeit schien alles vergeblich, bis endlich der Bürgermeister einen Ausweg fand.
sentences.l: For a long time all seemed in vain, until at last the burgomaster found a way out.
sentences.i: For a long time everything seemed hopeless, until at last the burgomaster hit on a way out.
sentences.n: “schien … vergeblich” = ‘seemed in vain.’ “Ausweg” = ‘way out, expedient.’

sentences.t: „Meine Meinung geht dahin,“ sprach er, „daß wir aus gemeinem Säckel diese Scheuer sammt allem, was darin liegt, Getraide Stroh und Heu, dem Eigenthümer bezahlen und ihn schadlos halten, dann aber das ganze Gebäude und mit ihm das fürchterliche Thier abbrennen, so braucht doch niemand sein Leben daran zu setzen.
sentences.l: “My opinion goes to this,” said he, “that we pay the owner for this barn, together with all that lies in it — grain, straw, and hay — out of the common purse, and hold him harmless, but then burn down the whole building and, with it, the dreadful creature, so that no one, after all, need stake his life on it.
sentences.i: “My opinion is this,” he said, “that out of the common purse we pay the owner for this barn and everything in it — grain, straw, and hay — and make good his loss, and then burn the whole building down, and the dreadful creature with it, so that no one need risk his life over it.
sentences.n: “Meine Meinung geht dahin, daß” = ‘my opinion is that.’ “aus gemeinem Säckel” — ‘from the common purse’ (Säckel, a small money-bag). “Getraide” = grain (1857 spelling of Getreide). “schadlos halten” = ‘to hold harmless, indemnify.’ “abbrennen” = ‘to burn down.’

sentences.t: Hier ist keine Gelegenheit zu sparen, und Knauserei wäre übel angewendet.“
sentences.l: Here is no occasion to be sparing, and stinginess would be ill applied.”
sentences.i: This is no time to be sparing, and penny-pinching would be out of place.”
sentences.n: “keine Gelegenheit zu sparen” = ‘no occasion to economize.’ “Knauserei” = ‘stinginess, penny-pinching.’ “übel angewendet” = ‘ill applied, misplaced.’

sentences.t: Alle stimmten ihm bei.
sentences.l: All agreed with him.
sentences.n: “stimmten ihm bei” — beistimmen (+ dat.), ‘to agree with, assent to.’

sentences.t: Also ward die Scheuer an vier Ecken angezündet, und mit ihr die Eule jämmerlich verbrannt.
sentences.l: So the barn was set alight at four corners, and with it the owl miserably burned up.
sentences.i: So the barn was set alight at its four corners, and the owl burned up wretchedly along with it.
sentences.n: “ward … angezündet” — passive, ‘was set alight’ (ward is the old preterite of werden). “an vier Ecken” = ‘at four corners.’ “jämmerlich” = ‘miserably, wretchedly.’

sentences.t: Wers nicht glauben will, der gehe hin und frage selbst nach.
sentences.l: Whoever will not believe it, let him go there and ask for himself.
sentences.i: Whoever won’t believe it, let him go there and ask for himself.
sentences.n: “Wers” = wer es, ‘whoever … it.’ “der gehe hin” — a jussive subjunctive, ‘let him go there.’ “frage … nach” — nachfragen, ‘to inquire.’ A common closing formula that winks at the reader.

glossary.ausziehen: ausziehen — to march out, set forth (against a foe) (infinitive; gegen den Feind ausziehen = to march out against the enemy; not ‘pull out, pluck out’)
glossary.besorgt: besorgt — anxious, worried (um jemanden besorgt sein = to be anxious for someone; here ‘anxious for his life,’ not ‘looked after, saw to’)
glossary.blicken: blicken — to look, glance; sich blicken lassen = to show oneself, appear (infinitive here, not the noun Blicke ‘looks, glances’)
glossary.muth: der Muth — courage, valor (1857 spelling of Mut; here ‘courage,’ not ‘mood, spirits’)
glossary.ungeheuer: das Ungeheuer — monster, huge creature (the noun here; not the adverb ungeheuer ‘enormously, hugely’)
